section_summary: This section is an excerpt from A History of Teachers’ Unions in Japan, followed by statistical tables, union demands, a collective bargaining agreement, membership lists, and a campaign chronology. It traces rival teachers’ unions from the May 1946 demonstrations through salary disputes and the cancelled February 1947 general strike to their June 1947 amalgamation. The appendices document teachers’ living costs, pay, membership, and negotiations with the Ministry of Education.

subfiles.title: Chapter 9: The May Demonstrations
subfiles.about: Zenkyo’s May 1946 demonstrations and confrontations with the Ministry of Education.
subfiles.summary: Zenkyo joined May Day activities and repeatedly pressed education officials for higher pay, food, reinstatement of dismissed teachers, and greater control of schools. Minister Abe and his successor Tanaka resisted its political demands and tactics. The chapter concludes that the confrontations produced no material gains, although they attracted some favorable press.

subfiles.title: Chapter 10: Attempts at Unification
subfiles.about: The failed June 1946 attempt to unite radical and conservative teachers’ unions.
subfiles.summary: Zenkyo and the Federation disagreed over political activity, demonstrations, and salary demands. At the 1 June meeting, a speech by Communist leader Nozaka prompted Federation delegates to withdraw, ending the proposed union conference.

subfiles.title: Chapter 11: National Unions and Their Subsidiaries
subfiles.about: The creation and expansion of competing national teachers’ unions in 1946.
subfiles.summary: Conservative unions formed the National League of Teachers’ Unions in June 1946, while Zenkyo reorganized as the Japan Educational Labor Union. Both sought prefectural affiliates. The radical union also pursued public support through groups promoting educational democratization, but the text reports limited growth for those groups.

subfiles.title: Chapter 12: Efforts to Obtain Higher Salary Scale
subfiles.about: Teachers’ pay campaigns, opposition to strike restrictions, and collective bargaining through March 1947.
subfiles.summary: Both national unions opposed a bill that would have barred teachers from striking, and teachers were removed from its provisions. Rival salary campaigns then sought a ¥600 minimum, allowances, equal pay for women, and bargaining rights. Radical teachers joined preparations for a February 1947 general strike, which a SCAP order stopped. The government offered temporary pay increases, and the Ministry of Education subsequently signed separate collective bargaining agreements with the rival unions.

subfiles.title: Chapter 13: Amalgamation of the Unions
subfiles.about: The June 1947 merger of rival teachers’ unions; page 24 is blank.
subfiles.summary: After the cancelled general strike, the League and Zen Kyo Kyo cooperated on protests and contract questions. They and independent unions merged at Nara on 8 June 1947 to form the Japan Educational Personnel Union. The author describes its leadership and program as favoring the conservatives’ more restrained approach.

subfiles.title: Appendix A: Retail Prices of Selected Articles, Tokyo, 1937–1942
subfiles.about: Prewar Tokyo retail prices for food, clothing, fuel, and other goods.
subfiles.summary: Lists annual prices for selected goods from 1937 to 1942, with units and a Tokyo Chamber of Commerce source.

subfiles.title: Appendix B: Livelihood of Teachers
subfiles.about: Estimates of teachers’ income, expenditure, and monthly deficits in 1945–1946.
subfiles.summary: A cited Civil Intelligence Section check sheet compares pay and household expenditure for teachers and university staff. It reports substantial monthly deficits and describes teachers’ reliance on savings, sales of possessions, and black-market activity.

subfiles.title: Appendix C: Salaries of Teachers in Relation to Rank
subfiles.from: Civil Information and Education Section, General Headquarters
subfiles.about: Teacher and education-official salary ranges by rank as of June 1944.
subfiles.summary: Shows rank classifications and representative annual salaries, citing Education in Japan.

subfiles.title: Appendix D: Cost of Living in Tokyo, April 1946–January 1947
subfiles.about: Monthly Tokyo household costs by spending category.
subfiles.summary: Tabulates food, housing, fuel, clothing, and other costs alongside a 1937 comparison.

subfiles.title: Appendix E: Tokyo Price Index for Wholesale and Retail Items
subfiles.about: Wholesale and retail price indices for selected periods through June 1946.
subfiles.summary: Compares aggregate and category price indices against a 1937 base.

subfiles.title: Appendix F: Tokyo Consumer Price Index
subfiles.about: Monthly consumer price indices from 1946 to August 1947.
subfiles.summary: Tracks rising effective prices, combining legal and black-market purchases across spending categories.

subfiles.title: Appendix G, Part 1: National League Demands
subfiles.about: The League’s demands for pay, allowances, equal treatment, and better working conditions.
subfiles.summary: Calls for a ¥600 minimum salary, equal pay for women, tax relief, larger allowances, and smaller classes.

subfiles.title: Appendix G, Part 2: Zen Kyo So Demands
subfiles.from: Council of All-Japan Teachers’ Unions to Secure a Minimum Standard of Living
subfiles.about: Seven demands submitted in October and November 1946.
subfiles.summary: Seeks a ¥600 basic salary, equal pay, tax relief, locality allowances, and an end to unlawful dismissals.

subfiles.title: Appendix G, Part 3: Five Additional Zen Kyo So Demands
subfiles.from: Council of All-Japan Teachers’ Unions to Secure a Minimum Standard of Living
subfiles.about: Additional demands concerning bonuses, allowances, tenure, and bargaining.
subfiles.summary: Requests year-end and family allowances, tax relief, youth-school tenure, and collective bargaining.

subfiles.title: Appendix G, Part 4: Zen Kyo Kyo Twelve-Point Demand
subfiles.about: The new council’s twelve-point program for pay and employment protections.
subfiles.summary: Demands a ¥600 basic wage, allowances, equal pay, protection from dismissal, bargaining, and private-school subsidies.

subfiles.title: Appendix G, Part 5: Thirteen-Point Demand of Government Employees’ Unions
subfiles.from: Council of All-Japan Government and Public Office Employees’ Labor Unions
subfiles.about: A joint labor program issued before the planned February general strike.
subfiles.summary: Seeks minimum wages, contracts, tax changes, repeal of labor restrictions, and apologies for arrests and remarks about labor leaders.

subfiles.title: Appendix G, Part 6: Government Answer to the Thirteen-Point Demands
subfiles.to: Council of All-Japan Government and Public Office Employees’ Labor Unions
subfiles.about: The government’s itemized response to the unions’ thirteen demands.
subfiles.summary: Promises inquiries and wage discussions, accepts rational contracts, rejects immediate repeal of labor legislation, and apologizes for a misleading phrase.

subfiles.title: Appendix G, Part 7: Additional League Demands
subfiles.about: Further salary and dependent-allowance demands after the strike was stopped.
subfiles.summary: Requests a 25 percent base-pay raise, a uniform ¥300 increase, and larger family allowances.

subfiles.title: Appendix H: Collective Bargaining Contract
subfiles.about: A provisionally signed agreement governing pay, hours, leave, personnel, union activity, and joint administration.
subfiles.summary: The Ministry recognizes the union as bargaining agent for its members and agrees to address pay, working hours, leave, medical care, personnel decisions, and union activity through specified procedures. It prohibits sex discrimination and certain dismissals, establishes a joint Council of Business Affairs, and encourages prefectural bargaining. The appendix bears a 19 March ministry heading but gives 3 March as the provisional signing date.

subfiles.title: Appendix H: Memorandum on School Staffing and Teacher Welfare
subfiles.about: Supplementary commitments on staffing, class size, tuberculosis care, maternity costs, and suspended teachers’ pay.
subfiles.summary: Promises staffing standards, classes below forty pupils, tuberculosis treatment facilities, maternity assistance, and full pay during suspension.

subfiles.title: Appendix I: Membership in the Two National Unions
subfiles.from: Civil Information and Education Section, General Headquarters
subfiles.about: Estimated and paid membership of the competing national teachers’ unions.
subfiles.summary: Compares national and Tokyo membership estimates and notes Hokkaido unions’ independence.

subfiles.title: Appendix J: Membership List of the Japan Educational Personnel Union
subfiles.from: Yoshihide Narita, Japan Educational Personnel Union
subfiles.about: Prefectural affiliates, headquarters addresses, and estimated teacher and union membership.
subfiles.summary: The table lists affiliated unions throughout Japan with their headquarters and estimated numbers of teachers and members. Its totals are 453,672 teachers and 446,151 members. A note says the post-merger chart illustrates both union strength and the way affiliates supplied statistics.

subfiles.title: Appendix K: Development of the National Unions
subfiles.about: A chart of teachers’ union formation, succession, and merger from 1945 to 1947.
subfiles.summary: Traces metropolitan and national unions into the June 1947 Japan Educational Personnel Union.

subfiles.title: Appendix L: List of Abbreviations
subfiles.about: Expanded names for teachers’ and government employees’ union abbreviations.
subfiles.summary: Defines abbreviations used for Tokyo and national unions and joint campaign bodies.

subfiles.title: Appendix M: Ministry Circular on Teachers Requesting Food
subfiles.from: Ministry of Education, Bureau of School Education
subfiles.about: A direction to stop teachers and school officials requesting food from pupils or parents.
subfiles.summary: Calls such requests harmful to families and directs school authorities to prohibit them.

subfiles.title: Appendix N: Ministry Circular on Teachers’ Self-Help Organizations
subfiles.from: Ministry of Education, Bureau of School Education
subfiles.about: Guidance on teachers’ self-help groups and political activity amid shortages and inflation.
subfiles.summary: Encourages self-help groups with limited restrictions while urging teachers to avoid disruption of education.

subfiles.title: Appendix O: Calendar of Teachers’ Salary Campaign
subfiles.about: A dated chronology of teachers’ salary campaigning from September through December 1946 in this section.
subfiles.summary: The calendar records rival unions’ meetings, demands, demonstrations, interviews, strike planning, and attempts to unite. It follows disputes over a ¥600 salary, equal pay, and cooperation with other government employees’ unions. The pages supplied end with the founding of Zen Kyo Kyo, its 23 December demonstration, and Iwama’s arrest and release; the chronology continues beyond this section.
